catalog_quote: Stress is phonologically unpredictable and is therefore phonemic. It is marked by a combination of intensity, length and pitch. ... Many words also have a definite secondary stress which occurs on the second syllable preceding the syllable with primary stress, and to a lesser extent on alternate syllables preceding this one. 4.2.1 Stress on nouns. Most two-syllable nonreduplicated nouns are stressed on the first syllable as shown in (18a, 19a), but some are stressed on the second syllable as shown in (18b, 19b). 18) a. /bʷalal/ ... 'floor' b. /bʷaˈla/ ... 'side of boat' 19) a. /hiwo/ ... 'fire' b. /hiˈwo/ ... 'there' ... Most three-syllable nouns are stressed on the penultimate syllable as shown in (22), although a small group are stressed on the final syllable as shown in (23). ... 4.2.2 Stress on verbs. Stress on verbs is generally predictable, and is closely tied to the transitivity of the verb. Whenever a verb root has both a transitive and intransitive form, the intransitive form is stressed on the penultimate syllable. The transitive form of some two syllable verb roots is formed simply by moving the stress to the final syllable as shown in (27-28). 27) a. /iˈgijal/ ... 'he dug' b. /igiˈjal/ ... 'he dug it' ... There is at least one pair of transitive verb roots which contrast in stress as shown in (33). 33) a. /iˈgabom/ ... 'he shared it out' b. /igaˈbom/ ... 'he broke it'

I read the page scan for pp. 7-8 directly (not just scanned) and the scanned for pp. 9-12. The quoted passage is on the page scan verbatim: p. 7 sec. '4.2 Stress' opens 'Stress is phonologically unpredictable and is therefore phonemic. It is marked by a combination of intensity, length and pitch. The stressed syllable is usually lengthened, especially when it is the first syllable of a two syllable word..'; then 'Many words also have a definite secondary stress which occurs on the second syllable preceding the syllable with primary stress..'; '4.2.1 Stress on nouns. Most two-syllable nonredup…
new_statements.rule_in_words: Author treats stress as phonemic (lexically/morphologically contrastive: 'bwalal 'floor' vs bwa'la 'side of boat'; 'hiwo 'fire' vs hi'wo 'there'; i'gabom 'shared' vs iga'bom 'broke'). Default pattern is penultimate: most 2-, 3- and all non-reduplicated 4-syllable nouns, intransitive verbs, most grammatical words. Final stress occurs in a lexical minority of nouns, in most transitive verb roots (transitives are regularly derived from intransitives by shifting stress to the final syllable, with or without vowel change/suffix), on the locative suffix -a (always stressed), exclamations, locative words, some numerals. Full reduplications carry stress on both halves; compounds take primary stress on the final stem.
new_statements.secondary_stress: 'Many words also have a definite secondary stress which occurs on the second syllable preceding the syllable with primary stress, and to a lesser extent on alternate syllables preceding this one' (p. 7); four-syllable nouns have secondary stress on the first syllable; prefixed verbs with final stress get secondary stress on the antepenult (p. 9).
new_statements.exceptions: Some 2-syllable nouns final-stressed; small group of 3-syllable nouns final-stressed; intransitives lomwan 'be hurting', hou'wa 'go first' are final-stressed; several transitive roots penult-stressed (i'kasi, i'bihi); one transitive minimal pair by stress (i'gabom vs iga'bom); reduplicated 2-syllable nouns stressed on both syllables with relative prominence depending on utterance position.
new_statements.domain_note: Word-level description from a ~2000-word corpus, citation forms and short utterances; explicit phrase-level effect: 'When a word which is usually stressed on the final syllable is utterance final, the primary stress is frequently moved to the antepenultimate syllable' (p. 11, exx. 42-43); sec. 4.3 treats statement/question/pause intonation separately. Data from Siagara village, Misima Island, 1978-80.
new_statements.identity_note: Callister 1993 describes 'Misiman' as a single language spoken on Misima, Panaeati and the eastern Calvados Chain islands (= Glottolog misi1243, ISO mpx); his data come from Siagara village on Misima Island (fieldwork 1978-80). The OPD sheet is titled 'Misima (Panaeati)'. No dialect differences in stress are mentioned. Fellows 1894 (not opened) concerns the Panaeati ('Pannieti') dialect specifically.

new_statements.quote: p. 73: "However, one common way to indicate undergoer focus is via shift of stress to the final syllable. Quite frequently there is also a vowel change in the final vowel." p. 77: "The third person singular forms are varied and it is not possible to predict them on phonological grounds. As a general rule for third person singular short clitics, undergoer referencing is indicated by a change in stress to the final syllable (Example 2)". p. 78: "Others however have stress on the penultimate syllable and are thus, in form, similar to the action focus form of other verbs." p. 96: "There are however some formal features that correlate with action focus, namely reduplication and penultimate stress." p. 98 n.1: "stress has been marked by the symbol "'" above the vowel of the stressed syllable e.g. án. new_statements.relation_note: Compatible with the catalog's existing statement from Callister 1993 (stress phonemic and phonologically unpredictable; intransitive verbs penultimate, transitive verbs final; locative -a attracts stress). The 1987 paper says the same thing about verbs in focus/transitivity terms (action focus = penultimate stress, undergoer focus = final stress; lexically determined) and adds detail the 1993 chapter lacks: the instrument suffix -iya always bears word stress and wins over the undergoer clitic; causative pa- forms; stress is a grammatical marker rather than a phonological rule. It says nothing about noun stress, so it neither confirms nor contradicts the 1993 noun statements.
new_statements.rule_in_words: A syntax paper on focus, not a phonology; it has no stress section but states repeatedly how word stress behaves on verbs. Stress is a grammatical marker: action-focus (intransitive) verb forms carry penultimate stress, and the commonest way to mark a third-person-singular undergoer (transitive/undergoer focus) is to shift stress to the final syllable, often with final-vowel change (i/a > e, u > o); the 3sg forms are 'lexically determined' and 'not possible to predict on phonological grounds'. The locative suffix -a (p. 88) and the instrument suffix -iya (p. 93, stress on the i) 'always' carry the word stress; when -iya co-occurs with an undergoer clitic the stress goes on -iya, not the clitic (p. 95). Causative pa- verbs keep penultimate stress unless the root ends in a consonant, in which case stress moves to the final syllable (p. 78, p. 98 n. 4). Stress is only marked in the examples where it is grammatically significant. Nothing on noun stress in general.
new_statements.exceptions: Monosyllabic verbs cannot show the final-stress undergoer marker (p. 78); some verbs have no overt 3sg undergoer marking and keep penultimate stress (p. 78, exx. 17-19); some verbs take suffix -an or -i instead of a stress shift (p. 78, p. 96); the instrument suffix -iya outranks the undergoer clitic for word stress (p. 95); causative pa- + consonant-final root shifts stress to the final syllable (p. 98 n. 4).
new_statements.identity_note: Callister 1987 describes 'the Misima language' of Misima Island (Milne Bay, PNG), the same variety as Callister 1993 (Siagara village fieldwork); no dialect is named in the 1987 paper.

sources.note: 'Suprasegmentals (tone, stress, length): Stress is phonemic. The stressed syllable is usually lengthened.' Examples i 'giyal 'he dug' vs i gi'yal 'he dug it'; i 'pani 'he climbed' vs i pa'ne 'he climbed it'. Also: plosives and /s/ may have nasal release utterance-finally in a stressed syllable.
